title: Air Quality and Early-Life Mortality: Evidence from Indonesia's Wildfires
research_question: What is the causal effect of severe air pollution exposure on fetal, infant, and early-child mortality, and how do these mortality effects vary across socioeconomic groups? Specifically, at what stage of early life (in utero versus postnatal) is exposure to particulate matter most damaging to survival?
data_description: The study combines multiple data sources at the Indonesian subdistrict-month level over December 1996 to May 1998 (3,751 subdistricts, 18 months, ~67,454 observations). The outcome is cohort size, measured as the count of surviving individuals born in a given subdistrict-month enumerated in the complete 2000 Indonesian Census of Population (used to infer 'missing children'). Air pollution is measured by the daily aerosol index from the Earth Probe Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer (TOMS), interpolated from grid points within 100 km of each subdistrict center and aggregated to monthly medians, means, and counts of high-smoke days. Auxiliary data include fire 'hot spot' locations from the European Space Agency, monthly rainfall from the Terrestrial Air Temperature and Precipitation dataset, household consumption from the 1996 and 1999 SUSENAS surveys, village-level fuel use and health facility counts from the 1996 PODES, food CPI from the central bank, and Census-based mother's education and urbanization measures.
institutional_context: Between August and November 1997, massive forest fires—predominantly set intentionally by logging companies and palm oil producers clearing land on Sumatra and Kalimantan—burned roughly 12 million acres of Indonesian forest. Unusually dry, windy conditions associated with El Niño caused the fires to spread out of control, and government firefighting efforts were largely ineffective until rains arrived in November. The fires blanketed much of Indonesia in dense smoke, with PM10 levels in the hardest-hit areas exceeding 1,000 µg/m³ on multiple days—far above the U.S. EPA 24-hour standard of 150 µg/m³. The geographic intensity of pollution depended on proximity to fires and on wind patterns, so northern Sumatra was heavily smoke-affected while Java was relatively spared. The episode provides sharp temporal and spatial variation in particulate exposure across pregnancy cohorts. The fires coincided with the onset of Indonesia's late-1997 financial crisis, and weak governance and crony ties (e.g., the Minister of Forestry's replacement by a timber magnate) limited accountability for firms that set illegal blazes.
